The professor clearly did not take his job seriously. Classes started a week late, then one week was lost to travel, another to unspecified reasons; as a result, neither the syllabus was completed nor the material properly understood. The core topics of the project were skipped with the excuse, “You’ve already seen this in ME342.” The limited material that was covered was rushed through at an unreasonable pace. Recording the lectures would have prevented this entire problem: no constant references to ME342, and no need for students to patch together knowledge from random sources.
Assignment deadlines were another mess. Extending each assignment two days before the deadline is not a favor; it simply disrupts students’ weekly plans. If delays are expected, reasonable deadlines should be set from the beginning.
The project evaluation was dominated by an obsession with “novelty.” In reality, academic work progresses largely through reproducing and building upon existing studies, which is why plagiarism detection software exists in the first place. In this context, it is unclear what level of “novelty” is realistically expected from a student project. Successfully reproducing a well-written paper should already be sufficient. Turning “novelty” into pressure on students serves no educational purpose and resembles a performative exercise rather than meaningful learning.
The Faculty of Mechanical Engineering has become the weakest engineering faculty at Bilkent. Poorly managed courses only worsen an already problematic situation. One has to wonder whether the university administration ever questions what a department that has existed for nearly twenty years is actually doing. “The ‘I can just walk away’ mentality must end. Otherwise the University's reputation is going to harmed in a serious way.
Finally, after a global pandemic where education functioned fully online across cities, insisting on hard-copy submissions of assignments and projects is difficult to justify.
